title: File Systems, Deadlocks, and Virtualization: Completing the OS Picture

questions.question: On Unix systems, where do a file's name and its metadata (inode) live?
options: Both are stored inside the inode
The name lives in the directory entry; metadata and block pointers live in the inode
The name is stored in the superblock; metadata in the FAT
Both are stored in the first data block of the file
questions.rationale: The inode stores size, timestamps, permissions, and block pointers; the file name lives in the directory — which is why multiple hard links can point at one inode.

questions.question: In linked file allocation, the main price paid is:
options: External fragmentation of the disk
Random access is slow because blocks must be followed one pointer at a time
A huge index block per file
The file system cannot track free space
questions.rationale: Linked allocation grows freely with no external fragmentation, but reaching block k means walking the chain from the first block, plus pointer overhead.

questions.question: What does a journaling file system do to survive crashes?
options: It writes the intended change to a log first, then applies it, replaying the journal after a crash
It keeps three copies of every file
It disables write caching on the disk
It stores all metadata in the inode
questions.rationale: Journaling (ext4, NTFS) logs the intended change before applying it, so a crash mid-write is repaired by replaying the journal rather than scanning the whole disk.

questions.question: Which of the following is NOT one of the four Coffman conditions for deadlock?
options: Mutual exclusion
Hold and wait
No preemption
Least privilege
questions.rationale: The Coffman conditions are mutual exclusion, hold and wait, no preemption, and circular wait; least privilege is a security principle.

questions.question: Why does breaking any single Coffman condition suffice to prevent deadlock?
options: Because all four conditions must hold simultaneously for deadlock to occur
Because conditions come in pairs
Because the OS kernel enforces at least one condition anyway
Because deadlock requires at least five processes
questions.rationale: All four conditions must hold at once; engineering away any one — e.g., requesting all resources at once kills hold-and-wait — makes deadlock impossible.

questions.question: The Banker's algorithm is an example of which deadlock strategy?
options: Prevention by breaking circular wait
Avoidance — granting a request only if the system stays in a safe state
Detection and recovery by killing a victim
The ostrich algorithm
questions.rationale: The Banker's algorithm is avoidance: it grants a request only while the system stays in a safe state, and it needs each process's maximum claim in advance.

questions.question: What is the 'ostrich algorithm' for deadlocks?
options: Killing the youngest process on each cycle
Detecting deadlock via the wait-for graph
Ignoring deadlocks because they are rare and prevention is costly — roughly what Linux and Windows do
Numbering all resources globally
questions.rationale: The ostrich approach ignores the problem — deadlocks are rare in practice and the machinery to prevent them is expensive, so desktop and server OSes largely ignore them.

questions.question: VMware ESXi and Xen are examples of which hypervisor type, and what does that type run on?
options: Type 2, running on a host OS like Windows
Type 1, running directly on the physical hardware
Type 2, running inside a web browser
Type 1, running inside a container
questions.rationale: Type 1 (bare-metal) hypervisors such as ESXi, Hyper-V, Xen, and KVM run directly on hardware and dominate data centres and clouds; Type 2 (hosted) ones like VirtualBox run atop a host OS.

questions.question: Docker containers achieve isolation primarily through:
options: A full guest operating system per container
Linux namespaces controlling what a process may see, and cgroups controlling what it may consume
Hardware virtualization extensions
Journaling the container's file system
questions.rationale: Containers share the host kernel; isolation comes from namespaces (visibility) plus cgroups (resource limits) — hence millisecond starts and megabyte sizes, but weaker isolation than VMs.

questions.question: In the cloud stack, which service model rents you the finished application itself?
options: IaaS
PaaS
SaaS
Hypervisor-as-a-service
questions.rationale: SaaS (e.g., Gmail) rents the finished application; IaaS rents raw VMs like EC2 and PaaS rents a managed runtime like Heroku — each level trades control for convenience.
